title: Bypassing CUDA for inference chips is inevitable, but SRAM's window may not stay open forever
dek: Training is a compute game, inference is a bandwidth game. Groq and Cerebras both bet on SRAM, but one discounts for determinism and the other discounts for yield; OpenAI chose the most expensive HBM4 because what it lacks is power, not money.
why: Two frontline chip entrepreneurs break down the trade-offs of the three paths taken by Groq, Cerebras and OpenAI, with plenty of engineering detail and cost accounting, for anyone who wants to understand what inference chips are really betting on.
who: Engineers and founders working on AI chips, compilers or inference infrastructure, and investors trying to understand the inference cost equation and heterogeneous approaches.
skip: From 1:13:03 to 1:14:47, Bill's startup advice to students is mostly personal reminiscence; you can fast-forward.

points.h: Training bets on compute, inference bets on bandwidth
points.body: In the training era no one could make money from training itself, so costs couldn't be quantified and everyone just wanted to bet on the strongest cluster; in the inference era the math is clear—how much the user pays per million tokens, and how much it costs me to produce those million tokens. More fundamentally, it's about computational density: training has massive data to saturate compute, while the decode phase of inference is strictly autoregressive, producing one token at a time, and each token produced requires reading the entire model from storage into the compute unit. So the core contradiction of inference shifts from compute to memory bandwidth.

points.h: SRAM is the consensus, but the two companies part ways
points.body: Groq and Cerebras both saw the bandwidth demand before Transformers appeared, and both converged on SRAM—because SRAM's absolute bandwidth and bandwidth per dollar are two to three orders of magnitude higher than HBM. The cost is capacity: DRAM stores one bit with one transistor plus one capacitor, while SRAM needs six transistors, so per-chip capacity may be two orders of magnitude lower than HBM. Thus the system must be scaled up, with hundreds or thousands of chips holding all model weights, and the bottleneck immediately shifts from capacity to cluster communication scheduling. Here the two diverge: Groq moves all scheduling ahead to compile time, while Cerebras simply stuffs a cabinet of chips into a single wafer.

points.h: Groq's static scheduling collides with MoE's dynamism
points.body: Groq designs hardware around the compiler, pushing determinism to the extreme with no runtime scheduling overhead. But after MoE appeared, each token activates 8 out of 128 experts, and which ones are chosen is decided at runtime, unpredictable at compile time. The static approach has only two options: either conservatively send all tokens and let some chips idle; or change the way the model is partitioned, but current models are hard to partition cleanly along dimensions other than experts. Idling only affects cost-effectiveness, not the fact that it's still fast, so Groq remains a good choice outside of GPUs.

points.h: The price Cerebras pays for yield
points.body: The maximum single-chip size is about 800 square millimeters, and a wafer can yield thirty or forty dies, so with 50% yield you still get 20 good ones. But Cerebras's entire wafer is one product, and if defects exceed the 30% it can tolerate, the whole wafer is scrapped. This isn't mask cost (masks can be amortized), but rather that out of every 10 made, maybe 9 are unusable. So it may achieve 10x Nvidia's bandwidth, but at 3x the cost of HBM, so bandwidth cost-effectiveness is discounted. Groq discounts for determinism, Cerebras discounts for yield cost, and the discounts ultimately hit token cost.

points.h: In the inference era, CUDA will definitely be bypassed
points.body: TPU and Trainium have no intention of being CUDA-compatible, yet people still find TPU software hard to use; Anthropic can buy in bulk because many of its engineers come from Google and know JAX. The key change is: in the training era people were willing to pay for good software, but in the inference era the balance tips toward performance and cost-effectiveness. As long as it's not many hard problems but one hard problem, writing all Transformer operators on a new chip makes business sense; plus AI coding accelerates operator optimization, greatly lowering the software stack barrier. DeepSeek would rather write low-level PTX assembly for optimization—that's the logic.

points.h: The faster the inference, the smarter the model
points.body: After agents exploded, a large number of tokens are not for humans to read but for other agents to read; human reading speed tops out at 100 tokens per second. But the significance of inference speed is not faster interaction, but that in the same minute of waiting, the model can use 10x more tokens for more internal thinking, thus becoming smarter. Jensen's slide has 'Smarter AI' on the horizontal axis and tokens per watt on the vertical. Conversely, some applications that give answers quickly may just be thinking less. Time is the fundamental constraint—ask AI to predict tomorrow's stock market, and if it thinks for two days, the answer is meaningless.

points.h: Grasp the invariants: FFN becomes stable after turning into MoE
points.body: Model structure will definitely affect chip design; for example, diffusion models are compute-intensive and suit another paradigm, so you first make a heterogeneous choice: whether to do this at all. More critically, find the invariants—in Transformers, the attention mechanism is still constantly innovating, with every new lab publishing papers with new ideas; but the FFN behind it has become a relative invariant since turning into MoE. RL in post-training also has no fundamental impact on model structure. So prioritize solving the part that has already converged, so the chip won't be left behind by algorithm iterations.

Bill Dally's exact words are that computer architecture is like real estate: everything is about location, location, location. Temporal locality means that after using a piece of data, you'll likely use it again; spatial locality means that after using a piece of data, you'll soon use the data around it. CPU caches are applications of these two. But in the decode phase of AI inference, algorithmic temporal and spatial locality are both flattened, so you must restore locality with hardware at the architecture level—putting model weights into SRAM is essentially buying the best locality.

points.h: OpenAI chose HBM4 because it lacks power, not money
points.body: Jalapeño is a general-purpose inference chip that packs prefill, decode, attention, and FFN all into one chip, and can even run game demos; the next generation will also support training. It stacks HBM4 bandwidth to 15.4 TB per second per package, taking the most expensive path. The reason is that U.S. data centers lack not capital and space but power, so it cares deeply about how many tokens can be produced per watt, and has done a lot of work on power consumption, with tokens per megawatt greater than Nvidia's corresponding Rubin architecture. In China, electricity accounts for about 1/3 of cost, in the U.S. about 2/3; different constraints lead to different convergence points.

points.h: Heterogeneity inside the chip, or at the system level
points.body: OpenAI proposed the concept of Dark silicon: when a chip does different things, some parts can be turned off or put into low-power mode, spending more cost to buy power efficiency. This differs from the system-level heterogeneity of Groq and Cerebras—the latter is one chip working with other chips, putting the attention KV cache on another chip. SRAM has poor capacity cost-effectiveness, suitable for storing fixed model weights, not for storing a continuously growing KV cache. So for scenarios where power is the first constraint, OpenAI's approach is great; for scenarios requiring extremely high bandwidth cost-effectiveness, it will still converge to SRAM.

quotes.text: In the training era, no one could rely on training to get any commercial return; training itself was something with no direct return.
This medium is not about the medium itself, but about focusing on the locality problem; you need to provide a higher level of locality than HBM.
When you can make something faster and cheaper than others, you won't tell people that your cost is actually cheaper.
In a mature company, it's still very difficult to disruptively push a research idea to the product team.

So faster inference doesn't mean you go from a minute of thinking to interacting in a second; rather, with the same one-minute interaction time, the model can use 10x more tokens for more internal self-thinking to improve its intelligence.
